questions.html:
The figure below illustrates the variation in the congestion window size of a TCP connection over time:

(On receiving 3 duplicate ACKs, the congestion window is reduced to half.)

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.html: TCP is in the slow start phase during the time periods \( t_0 - t_1 \), \( t_5 - t_6 \), and \( t_8 - t_{9} \).
TCP is in the congestion avoidance phase during the time periods \( t_0 - t_1 \), \( t_5 - t_6 \), and \( t_8 - t_{10} \).
TCP receives duplicate ACKs at time points \( t_2 \) and \( t_3 \).
TCP experiences timeouts at time points \( t_2 \), \( t_3 \), and \( t_9 \).

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

  1. TCP is in the slow start phase during $\mathrm{t}_{0}-\mathrm{t}_{1}, \mathrm{t}_{5}-\mathrm{t}_{6}$, and $\mathrm{t}_{8}-\mathrm{t}_{9}$.

    $\checkmark$ Correct - All three segments show exponential growth.
     
  2. TCP is in the congestion avoidance phase during $\mathrm{t}_{0}-\mathrm{t}_{1}, \mathrm{t}_{5}-\mathrm{t}_{6}$, and $\mathrm{t}_{8}-\mathrm{t}_{10}$.

    Incorrect - $\mathrm{t}_{0}-\mathrm{t}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{t}_{5}-\mathrm{t}_{6}$ are slow start, not CA.
     
  3. TCP receives duplicate ACKs at $\mathrm{t}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{t}_{3}$.

    $\checkmark$ Correct - Sudden drops to a value greater than $1 \Rightarrow$ Fast retransmit due to 3 duplicate ACKs.
     
  4. TCP experiences timeouts at $t_{2}, t_{3}$, and $t_{9}$.

    Incorrect - At $\mathrm{t}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{t}_{3}$ it's fast retransmit (duplicate $A C K s$ ), only $\mathbf{t}_{5}$ and $\mathbf{t}_{8}$ are timeouts (drop to 1 ).

questions.html: For a client-server application running over TCP or UDP, which of the following is true

options.html: the server program must be executed before the client program
the client program must be executed before the server program
the server program can be executed before or after the client program

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 7)

In a client-server application model:

  • The server is responsible for providing a service and must be running, or executed, first so that it can listen for incoming requests on a specific port.

  • The client is the entity that requests the service. It must be able to connect to the server's listening port to initiate communication (whether using TCP for a connection or UDP for sending a datagram).

 

If the client attempts to connect or send a request before the server is running and listening, the connection will fail, or the request will not be received. 

Therefore, the server program must be executed before the client program can successfully interact with it.

questions.html: Host $A$ sends two TCP segments to Host $B$ back-to-back. Host $B$ has already received bytes up to $110$. The first segment sent contains $100$ bytes with a sequence number $111$, and the second contains $10$ bytes. If the second segment arrives before the first, what will be the acknowledgment number sent by Host $B$ in response?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Host $B$ is still expecting byte $111$ (start of first segment). Since it has not received that yet, even if the second segment arrives early, it will discard it and acknowledge the last contiguous byte received $+1$ , which is $111$ .

questions.html: In TCP, define cwnd to be the congestion window size and rwnd to be the receive window size; the amount of unacknowledged data can not exceed
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Answer: C. min{cwnd, rwnd}

  • In TCP, the amount of unacknowledged data a sender can transmit is limited by the minimum of:

    1. The receiver's available buffer space (rwnd - Flow Control).

    2. The network's capacity (cwnd - Congestion Control).

  • Therefore, the Effective Window = $\min(cwnd, rwnd)$.

questions.html:
Professor Rao is explaining TCP congestion control to his students. He presents the following scenario:

  • A TCP sender is operating in the slow start phase.
     
  • The Maximum Segment Size (MSS) $=1000$ bytes.
     
  • Immediately after the $10^{th}$ ACK, the Congestion Window (CWND) is $2000$ bytes.
     
  • With this window, the sender transmits packets $11$ and $12$.
     
  • Now, the ACK for packet $11$ arrives.

According to TCP slow start rules, which new packets will the sender transmit at this point?

options.html: None (the sender must wait for more ACKs)

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 10)

  • At CWND = $2000$ bytes, the sender can keep $2$ packets in flight $\rightarrow$ packets $11$ and $12$.

 

  • When ACK for packet $11$ arrives, CWND increases by $\mathbf{+ 1}$ MSS ( $1000$ bytes) $\rightarrow$ CWND $=$ $3000$ bytes.

 

  • A $3000$-byte window allows $3$ packets in flight. Since packet $12$ is still outstanding, there is room for $\mathbf{2}$ more transmissions $\rightarrow$ packets $\mathbf{1 3}$ and $\mathbf{1 4}$.

questions.html: If a TCP sender has $14,600$ bytes of data in-flight (i.e., it has sent those bytes but has not yet received acknowledgment for any of them), which of these statements is NOT NECESSARILY true?

options.html: The congestion window size of the sender is at least $10$ MSS's (or, $14,600$ bytes)
The congestion window size of the receiver is at least $10$ MSS's (or, $14,600$ bytes)
The sender is expecting acknowledgment packets from the receiver
The flow control window advertised by the receiver to the sender is at least $14,600$ bytes

questions.solution:
Answer: A, C

Source solution 1 (score: 6)

If $14,600$ bytes are in-flight, the sender's congestion window must be at least $14,600$ bytes. So A is true. The receiver does not have a congestion window at all, it only has a flow-control window, so $B$ is not necessarily true. Since data is outstanding, the sender must be expecting ACKs, so C is true. For the sender to have sent $14,600$ bytes, the receiver's advertised window must be at least $14,600$ bytes, so $D$ is true.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

📌 Concept: TCP In-Flight Data

In-flight data = bytes that the sender has transmitted but for which no ACK has been received yet.

Two main windows control how much a TCP sender can transmit:

  1. Congestion Window (cwnd) – Sender-side; limits data based on network congestion detection.

  2. Receiver Window (rwnd) – Receiver-side; advertised in ACK packets; limits data based on receiver’s buffer space.

Sender's actual sending limit = min(cwnd, rwnd).

If in-flight = 14,600 bytes, then:

  • At the moment those bytes were sent, both cwnd and rwnd must have been ≥ 14,600 bytes (otherwise the sender wouldn’t have been allowed to send that much).

  • Also, the sender is definitely expecting ACKs for that data.

🔍 Options Analysis

A. The congestion window size of the sender is at least 10 MSS (14,600 bytes)

  • True, because cwnd must be ≥ in-flight data at time of sending.
    (This is necessarily true.)

B. The congestion window size of the receiver is at least 10 MSS

  • False concept – Receivers don’t have a “congestion window.” Congestion window is purely a sender variable.
    So this statement is not necessarily true – actually it’s meaningless in standard TCP.

C. The sender is expecting acknowledgment packets from the receiver

  • True – Unacknowledged data means the sender is waiting for ACKs.

D. The flow control window advertised by the receiver is at least 14,600 bytes

  • True – Because rwnd (advertised window) must have been ≥ in-flight at time of sending, otherwise sender would have stopped due to flow control.

✅ Final Answer: B

Reason: Congestion window is a sender-side mechanism; there is no “congestion window of the receiver.” Therefore, the statement is not true (and certainly not necessarily true).

questions.html:
You are watching a DVRUO Classes Computer Networks class in one browser tab, and you also open another tab to browse a cat-related blog. Both tabs establish TCP connections, and your laptop has only one IP address.

When a TCP segment arrives, how does the operating system decide whether it belongs to the DVRUO Classes lecture or to the cat blog, ensuring that packets don't get mixed up?

options.html: By checking only the IP address, since both tabs are on the same machine.
By using the port numbers in the TCP header, which let the OS map each segment to the correct socket/application.
By analyzing the application-layer data inside the payload.
By ordering packets based on their arrival timing.

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Correct Answer: B. By using the port numbers in the TCP header...

Explanation:

This problem tests your understanding of TCP Demultiplexing. Here is how the Operating System distinguishes between multiple network connections on the same device:

  1. IP Address is Insufficient: As stated in the problem, your laptop has only one IP address. All incoming traffic for both the video class and the cat blog arrives at this same destination IP. Therefore, the OS cannot distinguish the packets based on IP alone (ruling out Option A).

  2. The Role of Port Numbers: A TCP connection is uniquely identified by a 4-tuple:

    • Source IP

    • Source Port

    • Destination IP

    • Destination Port

  3. How it Works: When you open a tab for "DVRUO Classes," your browser assigns a unique, temporary source port (e.g., 5001) to that socket. When you open the "cat blog" tab, it assigns a different source port (e.g., 5002).

  4. The Return Path: When the servers send data back to you, they target these specific ports. The Operating System inspects the Destination Port in the TCP header of the incoming segment.

    • If the port is 5001 $\rightarrow$ send data to the Video Class tab.

    • If the port is 5002 $\rightarrow$ send data to the Cat Blog tab.

  • Option C is incorrect because the OS generally processes headers (Layer 3 and 4) to route packets; analyzing the application payload (Layer 7) for routing is inefficient and violates the layering principle.

  • Option D is incorrect because arrival timing is variable and cannot identify the recipient.

questions.html: Suppose that the advertised receiver window in TCP is $\mathbf{1}$ Mbyte long. If a sequence number is chosen uniformly at random from the entire TCP sequence number space ( size $=2^{32}$ ), what is the probability that the sequence number falls inside the advertised window?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

We are given:

  • TCP sequence number space $=2^{32}$.

 

  • Advertised receiver window size $=1 \mathrm{MB}=2^{20}$.


The probability that a random sequence number falls inside the advertised window is:

$$
\begin{gathered}
P=\frac{\text { Window size }}{\text { Sequence number space }} \\
P=\frac{2^{20}}{2^{32}}=\frac{1}{2^{12}}
\end{gathered}
$$

questions.html:
At some point, a TCP connection has the following state:

  • CWND = 4 MSS, SSTHRESH = $8$ MSS
     
  • All packets up to and including $\#411$ have been sent and acknowledged.
     
  • Packets $\#412$ through $\#415$ have been sent but not yet acknowledged.
     
  • Packets $\#416$ and later have not been sent.

Now, assume TCP is in Congestion Avoidance mode.

If an ACK for packet $\#412 $is received, which packet(s) will be sent as a result? (Select all that apply.)
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 8)

In Congestion Avoidance, each ACK increases CWND by about $1$/CWND.

Here CWND $=4 \mathrm{MSS}$, so after receiving an ACK it becomes $4+1 / 4 \approx 4 \mathrm{MSS}$ (rounded). This allows $4$ packets in flight. Since $\#413, \#414,$ and $\#415$ are already in transit, we can send $\#416$ to keep $4$ packets in flight.

Source solution 2 (score: 3)

Correct Answer: A. #416

Explanation: This problem asks us to determine the behavior of TCP in a specific mode ("Congestion Avoidance") given a specific state.

1. Analyze the Current State:

  • CWND: 4 MSS (Maximum Segment Size).

  • Unacknowledged Packets (In Flight): #412, #413, #414, #415.

    • Total in flight = 4.

    • The window is currently full (CurrentFlight=CWND).

  • Next Packet Sequence Number: #416 (waiting to be sent).

2. Analyze the Mode: The problem explicitly states: "Assume TCP is in Congestion Avoidance mode."

  • Note: Normally, if CWND(4)<SSTHRESH(8), TCP would be in Slow Start. However, in exam questions, explicit instructions override standard state assumptions. We must apply the rules of Congestion Avoidance.

3. Apply the Congestion Avoidance Algorithm: In Congestion Avoidance, the window grows linearly, not exponentially.

  • Growth Rule: For every ACK received, the CWND increases by CWND1​.

  • The Event: An ACK for packet #412 is received.

  • The Reaction:

    1. Slide the Window: The ACK tells us #412 has left the network. The "Flight Size" drops from 4 to 3 (packets #413, #414, #415 remain). This frees up 1 slot in the window.

    2. Grow the Window: Since we are in Congestion Avoidance, we increase CWND by a fraction:

      New CWND=4+41​=4.25 MSS

    3. Determine Send Count:

      • Effective Window Size (Integer) = ⌊4.25⌋=4.

      • Packets currently in flight = 3.

      • Available slots = 4−3=1.

    4. Result: The sender can send exactly 1 new packet.

Conclusion: The sender will transmit the next packet in the sequence, which is #416. It cannot send #417 yet because the window has not grown enough to accommodate a second new packet (that happens in Slow Start, where an ACK effectively opens 2 slots).

A TCP sender has MSS = $100$ B and a constant window size = $400$ B.

  • $p_{x}$: a packet whose first byte has the sequence number $x$.
     
  • $t_{x}$: time at which packet $p_{x}$ is transmitted.

At time $t_{1600}$, packet $p_{1600}$ (i.e., the packet containing bytes starting from 1600 ) has just been transmitted. What is the highest ACK received by the sender by this time?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Since $p_{1600}$ has just been sent, the end of the current window is at byte $1700$ . With a fixed window size of $400$ , the left edge (highest ACK received) must be $1700-400=1300$.

questions.html:
Alice is sending data to Bob over a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection in the congestion avoidance (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease) phase.

  • Maximum Segment Size (MSS) = $100$ bytes
     
  • Current Congestion Window (CWND) $=1000$ bytes
     
  • Alice sends a packet with sequence number $801$, and Bob replies with Acknowledgment $(A C K)=901$.

What will be the updated Congestion Window (CWND) after this acknowledgement?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 7)

In congestion avoidance, the congestion window increases by one MSS ( $100$ bytes) after all $1000$ bytes in the current window are acknowledged.

This means: if $1000$ bytes acknowledged $\rightarrow$ CWND increases by $100$ bytes.
So, if only $100$ bytes are acknowledged (as in this ACK), the increase is $(100/1000)$ of $100$ bytes $=10$ bytes.

Hence, new CWND $= 1000 + 10 = 1010$ bytes.
